title: Microfibre cloths: what they do, their limits and when to retire them
audience: Cleaners who dust, damp wipe and clean with microfibre cloths in residential, commercial, bond and short-stay work.
learningOutcomes: Explain how a microfibre cloth picks up soil, and why it works best when damp rather than wet.
Identify the product types and surfaces that limit where a microfibre cloth can be used.
Decide when a microfibre cloth is worn out and must be retired.
Keep microfibre cloths within the task and area system that the business has set for them.

instruction.heading: How the fibre does its work
instruction.body: A microfibre cloth is made from very fine synthetic fibres. Each fibre is thin, and the cloth as a whole presents a large surface, so it can take up fine particles that a looser cotton cloth would push around. The fibres also carry a light static charge, which helps them hold dust. Damp fibres draw liquid into the weave by capillary action. Those features make microfibre effective, and they work best when the cloth is damp. A dripping cloth carries water onto surfaces and floors. A dry cloth on a greasy surface may only move the film about. Treat the cloth as a tool that does its job at the right moisture level.

instruction.heading: Water first, and check the chlorine limit
instruction.body: The source material describes these cloths as suited to damp use with water alone, and it advises keeping them away from chlorine-based disinfecting products. This lesson records that advice as a source statement. Follow the supplier's written limits. The practical rule is the same either way. Read the label of any product before it goes near a microfibre cloth, and do not assume that a product safe on a hard floor is safe on a cloth. Use only the products the business has approved for the cloths, and keep the cloths stored away from chemical containers.

instruction.heading: Where microfibre works and where it does not
instruction.body: Microfibre suits routine upkeep on lightly soiled surfaces. On old or damaged surfaces the fibres catch on rough patches, and a snagging cloth can leave lint or drag. Heavy grease, dried-on residue and set-in soil need a different method or a stronger approach, and the job should not be forced with a microfibre cloth. The source also notes that relying on microfibre for a single job, for example high dusting, may not give the best result. A cleaning system that uses the cloths across several tasks, with cloths assigned by area and by task, gives better and more consistent results than ad hoc use. Set the tasks in the business standard rather than leaving them to habit.

instruction.heading: Folding, refolding and cloth-use rules
instruction.body: Use one face of the cloth at a time. Fold it so that a clean face is ready while the previous face loads with dust or soil, and refold as each face fills. The source gives a rule of thumb that a standard cloth provides about eight usable faces and that one cloth is normally enough for one area or one room. That is historical hospital practice, not a rule for every job. Treat it as a first guide, then set the business's own cloth-use rule from how quickly each cloth loads, the surfaces it covers and the soil level of the area. Where two areas share a cloth, cross-contamination control under “Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart” applies.

instruction.heading: Retiring a worn cloth
instruction.body: Retire a microfibre cloth when it no longer lifts dust or residue as it did, when its fibres have torn or pilled, or when it has snagged a surface. A cloth that has been used on a dirty area does not return to a clean area, however it looks after washing. Move retired cloths out of the clean set and into the used-cloth route the business sets. Where the business tracks cloth life, record early failures, because a run of them points to a laundering fault, a wrong product or a surface that is too rough for the fibre.

instruction.heading: The environmental claim, stated carefully
instruction.body: It is tempting to assume that a water-dampened cloth uses less product than a sprayed or soaked method. The source describes the water-dampened design but does not measure product use, so this lesson does not claim a saving. Whether microfibre reduces product use on a given job depends on the surface, the soil, the dilution and the method, and it has not been measured in this draft. If the business wants to make an environmental claim, it should first measure product use and waste on its own jobs. Until then, treat the water-dampened method as a cleaning technique and not as evidence of a lower environmental impact.

procedure: Check that the cloth is clean and in good condition, then dampen it to the damp state the job sheet requires, wringing out any surplus water.

Confirm the product on the job sheet is one the business has approved for microfibre cloth use, and read its label. Stop if the product is chlorine-based and the approved list or the supplier's written limit does not allow it.
Fold the cloth so that a clean face is ready, and use one face at a time.
Work the cloth across the surface in the set order, moving to a clean face as each one fills.
After wiping, look at the surface. If the cloth leaves lint or the surface snags, stop, change the method and record the surface for the supervisor.
Retire any worn cloth into the used-cloth route, and store the clean cloths away from chemical containers.

workedExamples.situation: A short-stay turnover. You clean a bathroom vanity and then the kitchen bench, and you use the same cloth for both.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should you do with the cloth, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not carry one cloth from zone to zone. Set the bench cloth aside for the bench and the bathroom cloth for the bathroom, using the colour and area system in “Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart”. Keeping the sets apart stops soil from the bathroom reaching the kitchen.

workedExamples.situation: A commercial office has a reception top made of old timber. The cloth you used on the foyer glass snags on the worn finish and leaves lint.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop on that surface. Change the cloth and review the method for the finish. Tell the supervisor that the surface is worn and the cloth is snagging, and record the finding. Do not keep forcing the cloth across the surface, because that damages the finish and wears out the cloth.

workedExamples.situation: A bond clean. You are asked to remove a mark from a kitchen bench, and the only product to hand is a chlorine-based product that you would wipe on with a microfibre cloth.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the microfibre cloth with the chlorine-based product unless both the supplier's written limit and the business's approved list allow it. Use the approved product and cloth set for that surface. Check the label before any product touches the cloth, and report the missing product to the supervisor.

equipmentAndPpe: Microfibre cloths assigned to the area and the task
Approved cleaning product from the job sheet, with its label read
Used-cloth bag or laundry route set by the business
Gloves and any PPE the product label lists
Warning sign where a wet surface or a fall risk has been created

commonErrors.error: Using a dripping cloth, which carries water onto the surface, the floor and the fittings.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the cloth damp, not wet, and wring out the surplus before use.

commonErrors.error: Using one cloth across several tasks until it is loaded.
commonErrors.prevention: Refold to a clean face as each one fills, and retire the cloth when it no longer picks up soil.

commonErrors.error: Using a microfibre cloth with a chlorine-based product without checking the limit.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the supplier's written limit and the approved list first, and use an approved product.

commonErrors.error: Forcing a snagging cloth across an old or damaged surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, change the method and record the surface for the supervisor.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Product use follows the label and the safety data sheet. Checking whether a product is suitable for a microfibre cloth is part of that label check, not a shortcut around it.
Wet surfaces and wet floors created by wiping are a slip hazard. Warning signs stay in place until the area is dry.
The source cites two UK publications on microfibre (2006 and 2007). They were not read for this draft and are not relied on in this lesson.

qualityStandard: Cloths are used damp, not dripping, on the surfaces that the job sheet names.
No product is used with a microfibre cloth unless the product is approved for the cloth and its label has been read.
Cloths stay within their assigned area and task set, with no cross-zone use.
Worn or snagging cloths are retired, and a surface where a method fails is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Cloth set and task assignment shown on the job sheet.
Record of any cloth retired early, and of any surface where a microfibre cloth snagged, with the fix.
summary: Microfibre picks up fine soil best when it is damp, not wet.
Check the product label before any product touches a microfibre cloth.
Use each cloth within the business's task and area system, and refold to a clean face as each one fills.
Retire a worn or snagging cloth, and never return it to a clean area.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which moisture level suits a microfibre cloth for damp wiping a bench?
options: Dripping wet, so that the cloth lifts more soil today
Damp, not dripping, so that water does not run onto the floor
Dry on every surface, including greasy ones and dry on the floor too

knowledgeChecks.question: The cloth leaves lint and catches on an old timber top. What is the correct action?
options: Press harder so that the cloth grips the surface
Stop, change the method, and record the surface for the supervisor
Finish the job and mention the marks to the customer at the end

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about product use with microfibre cloths is correct under this lesson?
options: Any product that is safe on a hard floor is safe on a microfibre cloth
Check the label and the approved list before any chlorine product is used.
A water-dampened cloth saves product, so the approved list can be skipped

sourceReferences: Cleaning Operations Manual, Long Bay Hospital, dated 18/04/2012 (file named Green-Cleaning-Manual2012), sections: Cleaning with microfibre cloths, and the microfibre task sheet; rights: user-held (reworded, no copying). Historical 2012 hospital practice, including the one-cloth-per-area and eight-faces rules, which are not used as current instructions.

UNCONFIRMED: the source's statement that microfibre cloths should not be used with chlorine-based disinfectant cleaners has not been checked against current supplier or product-label guidance. Date checked: none.
